title: Airport Route Finder: Non-Stop Routes
description: Check any two airports in the Airport Route Finder: is there a non-stop route in the OpenFlights dataset, or a one-stop option via a hub? Free.
summary_sentence: For example, JFK to LAX comes back as a non-stop in the dataset, while smaller airports are answered with one-stop options through the hubs that actually serve them.
quick_answer: The Airport Route Finder checks two airports against the OpenFlights route dataset and answers a simple question: does a non-stop route exist between them, and if not, which hub airports connect them with one stop? Type two IATA codes and read the verdict with great-circle distances for each leg.
steps_intro: Airline route maps are marketing; a dataset is an answer. Three steps to a checkable verdict:

use_cases.title: Testing a trip idea before booking sites

body.t: Before fighting with booking engines, learn whether your pair is even a non-stop. If it is not, the hub the finder names is usually the connection the airlines will sell you anyway.
A slightly further airport with a non-stop often beats the near one plus a connection. Run both pairs and let the route structure, not the drive, make the decision.
Network questions — which cities are one stop from everywhere, which regions depend on a single hub — start with pair checks like these against a fixed dataset.
Travel arrangers can answer “is there a direct flight?” with a dataset verdict rather than a shrug, and quote the one-stop hub in the same breath.

JFK → LAX (approx. 3,974.3 km, 2,469.5 mi): the dataset lists non-stop service, as expected on a flagship transcontinental pair. The finder still earns its keep — it proves the assumption instead of repeating it.

Heathrow → Frankfurt (approx. 653.5 km, 406.1 mi) is non-stop in the dataset, while many regional pairs of similar length are not — density of service follows demand, not distance. That contrast is exactly what the tool exposes.

popular_table.note: Verdicts come from the OpenFlights dataset snapshot the tool ships; a route's absence means the dataset lacks it, which the FAQ explains how to sanity-check.

faq: No. The finder reads the OpenFlights route dataset — a community snapshot of routes airlines operate — not today's timetables. It answers “does this route exist in the network”, not “what flies on Tuesday”.
Why might a real route be missing?

Datasets age: new routes appear, seasonal routes pause, and small carriers are unevenly covered. If a booking engine sells a non-stop the finder lacks, trust the booking engine and treat the dataset as the thing that is out of date.
What does one-stop via a hub mean?
No non-stop exists in the dataset for your pair, but airport H exists with routes to both sides, so A → H → B is a bookable shape. The finder names the hubs rather than inventing a connection.
No — the tool answers non-stop and one-stop only, which covers the large majority of practical itineraries and keeps the answer honest.
Are the distances road or air?
Air: each leg's great-circle distance between airport coordinates, the same model as the Airport Distance Calculator.
Do alliances matter to the result?

The dataset records operating routes regardless of alliance. In practice one-stop suggestions are most useful when the hub is served by the same alliance you plan to book with — check that at booking time.
Can I use city names instead of IATA codes?
The finder is built around IATA codes (JFK, LHR, CDG). If you do not know a code, the Airport Distance Calculator's search resolves names to airports first.
